The Sadiya Frontier Tract is the North-East Front- in* and ier Distriot of India, bordering on Tibet on the north bouadana*. and east and on Bnrma on the south and south-east. The Distriot was formed in 1912 with headquarters at Sadiya and with the old Sadiya Subdivision of the Lakhimpur Distriot as a nucleus, under the name “ Central and Eastern Seothms, North-East Frontier," whioh was later ehanged to the present designation. It lies between 27 ° 15 ' and 29° north latitude and 94° 15 " and 97° east longitude, extending from the Subansiri river on the west to the Lohit-Brahmaputra-Irra- wady watershed. It includes the mountains on the southern faoe of the main Himalayan Divide, the west- ern and north-western slopes of the Dapha and Fhunkan ranges, which separate India from the extreme north of Burma and crosses the Patkoi Range to touoh the northern end of tho Hawkong Valley and run with the eastern portion of the unadministered area of the Naga Hills. Exoept where the distriot touches Lakhimpur, i.e., on the south, its boundaries have not

been . demarcated, following mainly as they do the principal ridges of tumbled masses of mountains, whioh form the eastern extremity of the Himalayan system. The area of the Tract is some 10,000 square miles, of whioh 3,500 square miles are under regular administra- tion. The latter area represents the plains and foot hills. The boundaries officially notified are as follows : — “ From Siplumukh on the Subansiri east along the ridge of the outer range to the Jiya Dhol river ; thsnoe down the right bank of the Jiya Dhol river to where it eats the Rajgarh Ali ; thence east along the foot of the bills following the village path running along the foot of the hills so as to include all Galong villages to the Dipa (8inyang) N.» east-south-east of Dipa village; thence down the right bank of the Dipa (Sinyang) N. to its confluence with the Si men river ; thence down the right bank of the right channel of the Simen river to where it unites with the left channel to form one 6tream ; thence across and down the Simen (Dijmur) river to its confluence with the Burhi Suti ; thence east along the left bank of the Burhi Suti to the Sengajan road ; thence south-east along the Sengajan road to the Brahmaputra ; thence east along the right bank of the Brahmaputra so as to include Mesaki G ha pari to the point where the Burhi Suti Channel takes off from the Brahmaputra river east of Pomua Tillage ; thence across the Brahmaputra so as to include Dorkang and Kaplang Chaparis and along the Laika Jan to its common junc- tion with the Mora Laika Jan and Ajuka N.; thence up tho Ajuka N. to its junction with a small feeder stream connecting the Ajuka N. with the Dangori N. ; thence along the Dangori N. to its junction with the Dhole or Daokhati N. ; thenoe along the Dhola or Haokhati N. to a point (marked by a post; whence it runs south- wards, marked ' 450 ’ on the 1-inch to 1 mile map, the post being about one mile due west of Ohhota Dirak village, which is situated on tho Dirak Hka ; thenoe along the southern edge of the track running approxi- mately eastwards to the Dirak Hka so as to exclude Clihota Dirak village ; thenoe south-east up the left bank of the Dirak Hka to where it is orossed by the village path from Mohanggaon to Bara Dnmsa ; thenoe southwards along this path to Bara Dumsa and Bisa Pathar and along the western limit of Bisa Pathar and down tlie left bank of the Kolia or Koriapani (stream) to the Burhi Dihing or Namphuk river ; thenoe up the right bank of Burhi Dihing or Namphuk river to immediately opposite the Namonik confluence ; thenoe

up the left bank of the Namohik river to the Namchik- Kathang Hka confluence ; thenoe up the Tfntliung Hka to the Kathang Hka-Lekha Hka oonfluenoe, thenoe up the Lokha Hka to its source at hill 894 ; thenoe down a small stream following a south-westerly direction to the Tirap river, thence up the Tirap river to its western souroe (Satnhak Ju) and the Patkai ridge ; thenoe east- wards (in conformity with the agreement between the Assam Government and the Government of Burma as to the interprovinoial boundary).” 3 The general appearance of the Distriot is that of * r * 1 mighty mountains oyerhanging tree-covered plain and app * Mmnc *‘ of grassy expanse everywhere intersected — far west by large river beds and water oourses whloh merge from atony submontane tracts into sandy alluvial plains covered with forest and gigantio grasses. The mountains are very steep and the river* debouching from the higher levels splay over miles of oountry. The whole area is very sparsely populated with but little of the older alluvial soil whioh constitutes the wealth of Assam. Communications are mainly on the surface of the rivers or else hug their banks, and such villages as there are are confined to the neighbourhood of the main rivers. The sandy plains carry poor forest, the Sitnul tree (Bombax Malabaricum) being tlie main feature. On the higher levels evergreen forest prevails but the more valuable species are not found in profusion. The main artery of the province — the Brahmaputra Mountain river — enters Assam in tne Sadiya District. Rising near the Monasorowar lake, away north of Kashmir 3 it flows eastward as the Tsangpo through Tibet, being crossed by the India-Lhassa road at Ghaksara ferry, not far horn Lhaasa and then turns southward cutting the main Himalayan axis at a point of which the approxi- mate latitude is 29'35° and longtitude 95‘20°. In its bend it encircles some magnifioent peaks dominated by Namoha Barns (24,446'), at the northern foot of which lies, west and east, the gorge in whioh were supposed to exist the falls whioh remained a geographical mystery until 1918, when the area was explored by Captains Bail- ey and Morahead.* No falls were discovered but a series of rapids for thirty miles. The Tsangpo receives many tributaries in its oonrse through the Abor Hills, the Bingong, Sirapateng (Sigong), 8himong, Siyom, Yamne and as known So the Abors as the Slang. It leaves the hills and enters the plains at Pasighat. A few miles • 71m most MaS*d and reliable information amiable on the Tmagpo

faXUie that of the Ward-Cawdor Expedition, 1984*90, which Wetted, examined and mapped the oourse of the rim thragh the gorge. Annamte Os page 4 brdow Pnsigbat it divides into two channels — the Dihong channel and the Lalli — the island between, known as the Lalli Cliapri, being a game reserve. Twenty miles south of Pasighat and west of Sadiya it is joined by the LoMt-Brahmaputra. The Lohit rises in eastern Tibet where it is known as the Zayul and flows southward entering the distriot twenty-five miles south of Rima which is situated on the left bank. Thirty miles further south it turns due west at Minsang. In its course it receives many addi- tions the Dou, Delei, Tidding, Digaru, Dibong, Kamlung, Noa Dehing and many smaller rivers which carry off the drainage of the huge mountain systems on both sides of its bed. The Lohit-Brahmaputra is known to the Mishmi tribes as the Tellu and in its journey through the hill section of the Frontier Tract flows through the Mishmi country and enters tlie plains at Farsuramkund, forty-six miles from Sadiya, a place of pilgrimage for Hindus. The Dibong which joins it a short distance below Sadiya drains the mountain masses north of Sadiya and is notable for the deep gorges and inhospitable oountry of its upper reaches. Feeder steamers can pass up the Brahmaputra at. all seasons as far as Murkong Selek which lies 40 miles upstream from Dibrugarh, while from May to Nov- ember they can penetrate a further fifty miles. As can be readily understood, the river is subject to big floods and at snch times the junction between Sadiya and Kobo of the main stream and its two ohief confluents, the Lohit and the Dibong, is a sight of savage relentless strength and beauty. The actual bed of the river is wide and in the cold weather it winds among huge sand banks or * ohapris 9 (islands of pure formed by the river and covered by grass or small tree jungle). The river is oontinually changing its oourse within its bed, eroding both banks in turn, this erosion has already destroyed one Sadiya and is even now a source of imminent danger to the existing town. 5 Communications in the plains are largely by river. Comoran »• All the important bazaars, Sadiya, Saikhoa, Kobo, catl0n, ‘ PasighatAdurkong Selek, are looated on the Brahma* putra.V'The Assam Trunk Road (south bank) enters the District at mile 321, near Dholl a village and reaches

the Lobit-Bmhmaputra at Saikhoaghat 821th mile and used to reappear on the north bank where formerly for 3$ miles it .continued to Sadiya. Most of the north hank section* of the Bond has however disappeared into the river. Hoads radiate from Sadiya. One goes north to Nizamghat (31 miles) running parallel and close to the Dibong river, vid Kirim, Bolung and Mishmi Bomjur villages. It serves as an outlet for the Dibong and Si6sori villages and is passable for carts and light motor cars during the cold weather, November to May. A cart road runs to mile 21$ east where it bifurcates and thence (1) a cold weather cart road goes, vid Digarumukh (3} miles) and Tizumukh (14$) to Temai (23$ miles) whence orossing the Lohit- Brahmaputra (Parsu- ramkund) is 4 miles by bridle track. (2) The second is the Lohit Valley road to Tidding river (77 miles), vid Paysn (mile 86, cart road), and thereafter Tiki, Chikorpani, Denning, Dreyi and Theronliang, five stages by bridle traok, each some 10 miles in length with furnished bungalows at each stage. Between Dreyi (5,200') and Theronliang the road orosses the Tidding Saddle (6,000') and drops 4,000 feet in 8 miles of bridle track. On a clear day a fine view of the plains is obtainable from Dreyi. The other main road in the District oonneots Kobo with Pasighat (21 miles) t id Pillung (11} miles), furnished inspection bungalows being found at all three places. This road continues as a bridle traok into the Dihong Valley along the right bank of the river, vid Rengging (miles 18} on bridle traok), Rotung (23 miles) to Tembung (88 miles) where Frontier outposts are stationed in the oald weather. About two miles from Tembung, on the left bank of the river is the memorial cairn to Dr. Gregorson who was treacherously murdered here by some Mmyang Abora in March 1011. A similar cairn 6 Otology. marks the actual spot where Mr. Noel Williamson, Assistant Political Officer, whom Dr. Greg orson was accompanying, was similarly murdered at Komsing, 6 miles further on. From Kobo a surface road leads to Murkong Selek (7 miles) , where are found the Veneer Mills of the Assam Saw Mills and Timber Company. From Saikhoagbat railway station a surface cart road also leads to tho vicinity of Rongdoi Miri village (12J miles) on the left bank of the Brahmaputra immediately opposite Kobo, which is itself twenty-five miles down-

stream from Sadiya. Owing to the many large rivers the maintenance of through road communications is almost impossible. Saikhoaghat railway station, the terminus of the Dibru- Badiya Bailway which connects with the Assam-Bengal Bailway at Tinsukia junction, is rail head for the Sadiya Frontier Tract. It is separated from Badiya, the distriot headquarters, by six miles of the river bed of the Brahmaputra. The normal link of communica- tion is the common dugout ferry of Assam, supplemented by the “ mar ” for vehicles, the time and traok distance over sand depending on the state of the river. The ferry crossing on the north bank is at Parghat where the Assam Trunk Boad, to which previous reference has been made, reappears three miles from Sadiya. Saikhoaghat is also rail head for Kobo and Murkong Selek. Those interested in the geological formation of the Tract will find available information in the various Beoords and Memoirs of the Geological Survey of India and in Colonel Burrard and Sir Henry Hayden’s -account of the Himalayas. Through .the klndnees of the Assam Oil Company, a short aooount of the geology of the portions of the Sadiya Frontier Tract examined by the geologists is also available, and has been appended as an annexnre to this volume. 7 The olimate on the whole compares favourably with the rest of Assam, and Sadiya has a good reputation for health among Indians in general. There is a reason* able rainfall, and the snow-covered mountains visible from the river not only add to the natural beauty of the place but are the souvoe of the melting snows whioh flood the rivers and soften the fierce heat of the summer season. There are, however, great variations in rainfall, very high figures being recorded at places close to the hiUa. Thus Pasighat averages some 200 inohes yearly or double that of Sadiya. At places like Pasighat where the large rivers debouch on the plains, regular gorge winds occur nightly for months on end. The Pauna is well varied, but no speoies occurs in any great number exoept possibly wild elephant, buffalo and tiger. Sambhur, hog deer and harking deer are found. The wild mythan is rare, as is also the swamp deer of Assam ; in fact the existence of the latter was doubted until reoently. The monkey tribe is Btrongly 1 “presented, the hoolook and other kinds being found on the hill* as well as on the plains. The hoolook is sacred

to some of the tribes who, as a rule, have few soruples as to their food. There is not a single specimen of the rhineoeros left, yet at one time both the Rhinooeros Indie us (the one horned Asiatic Rhinoceros) and ano- ther small kind were found, the latter possibly the Ceralorhinus Sumatrensis (small, two horned). All have been shot out by the tribesmen for their meat, hide and horn previous to our intimate administration. The domesticated mythan is very oommon among all the tribesmen and is the chief standard of wealth and barter. The Abors breed it largely for sale. That Zoological cariosity the ' takin ’ (Budoroas Taxioolor) is found in the Mishmi hills from 4,000 feet upwards. This animal is essentially a serow with affinities to the bovines through the musk ox and other relationships with the •heep goat and * antelope ’ (J. Oookburn). The Bin* turong (Articnrus Bintnrong) has been shot. The wild dog, the larger speoies, is not much in evidence. Small game birds are disappointing. ITorioan have practically Climate. Fauna. 8 disappeared, but the monaul and the blood pheasant are found in the distant hills. Partridge are praotioally non- existent and snipe are rare, but green pigeon afford good sport in the month of August. Geese and duck are met with in large numbers on the Brahmaputra and Dihong during their returning flight to Tibet and Central Asia. The rivors were famous for their mahseer but in the accessible areas the fish seem to have grown sophisti- cated. Wild elephant are fairly common and aro a good source of revenue to Government, 128 being oaptured in 1922-23. Herds of wild buffalo are found near Sanpura which inter-breed with the village buffa- loes let loose by the Khamtis, after the completion of the rioo cultivation. CHAPTER II. HISTORY. Introdnotion. The following rdsumd of the history of the hill tribes of the North-East Frontier and their relations to the British at Sadiya is in continuation of Chapters II and III of the Lakhimpur District Gazetteer in which an account of all frontier affairs up to the year 1905 will be found. It will perhaps enable the reader to understand more readily the great changes which have ooourred since 1905, if we divide the twenty years now to be dealt with into three distinct periods. The first is that of Mr. Williamson’s tenure of the post of Assistant

Political Offloer, Sadiya, under the old rdgimd. The seoond deals with the years of great activity on the North-East Frontier, consequent on Mr. Williamson's and Dr. Gregorson’s murder by the Minyong Abors in Maroh 1911. The third shows the progress of the new Frontier Distriot, the formation of which was shewn to be neoessary, as a result of the above-mentioned activities. A 8 regards the first period, the suooess whioh mark- et offiteT ed Mr. Williamson's work at Sadiya may be summarised in the words used in the Political Report on the Abor expedition—" it opened a new era in our relatione with 9 the hills.” In the course of a little more than five* years the Assistant Political Offioer, Sadiya, carried through a series of remarkable tours, all of which were* most fruitful, both in establishing more friendly rela* tions with the hill tribes and in increasing our know* ledge of their idiosyncrasies and of the geography of the difficult country in which they live. It would be tedious here to recount all of these numerous tours, but a few of the more important should be mentioned. In December 1907 the Assistant Political Offioer journeyed up the Lohit river as far as Sati, the last Miju village in* the direction of Tibet. He travelled entirely on local transport and was everywhere rcoeived hospitably. In the same year he had toured through the foot hill villages lying between the Dihang river and the Simon river (Dijmur). In January and February 1908, a friendly visit was paid to Kebang, a Minyong Abor village lying three marches up the Dihong river from Pasigliat^ which had not been visited by a British officer since the disastrous expedition of 18o8. In November and December of the same year, Mr. Williamson led a small expedition into the Kangpang Naga Hills to exaot punishment from the village of Rashi which had raided she British Naga village of Wakpmg in October 1907, killing seven British subjeots. During this tour a con- siderable area of previously unknown country was roughly surveyed and a point reached from which the Hukawng Valley was clearly visible. In the cold weather of 1909-10, a second tour up the Lohit was. made during which the Assistant Political Officer had an interesting meetiug with the Tibetan officials of Bima. Throughout this period our relations with theB*istfcnr Tarnon, Miju and Digaru Mishmis remained uniformly satisfactory. Tho Assistant Political Offioer was mater-

ially assisted by the leading Khamti Chief, Chowna Oohain * in his tours up the Lohit Valley, and the beha- viour of the Khamtis and Singphos continued to be good The Chnlikata Mishmis also gave no trouble, * Since deopastd. 10 though with the exception of certain exempted villages, the tribe as a whole was blockaded as a punishment for their failure to capture the Bebcjia Mishmi raiding gang led by Pongon Midcrcn of Elapoin. These savages had in 1905 killed three Dowaniya British subjects at Dikrang, a few miles from Sadiya, in revenge for Pongon’s impri- sonment during the 1900 Bebojia expedition. The Bebcjias were blockaded throughout this period but none of the murderous gang was arrestod. Mr^Mun • ^ktions w ith the Padam Abors also continued »on ud Ur* satisfactory, but the conditions existing on the right Grvoroon. bank of the Dihang liver, where the l’asi-Minyong villages overlook the plains, caused the Assistant Political Officer considerable anxiety. The disquieting state of affairs on this section of the Erontier was not, to use Mr. Williamson’s words, entirely the fault of the Pasi-Minyong Abors, and it was in order to establish our relations with those tribesmen on a firmer and more friendly footing that the Assistant Political Officer made many tours among these tribes- men, on the last of which he and most of his party were murdered at Komsing on March 31st. 1911. His companion Dr. Gregorson and some sick followers who had been left behind at Pangi village had been previously killed. It would be out of place to explore the very numerous contributing causes which led to this massacre, but the act which certainly preci- pitated it, was the murder, by men of Rotung village, of a Miri named Manpur and three sick coolies who had been sent book with letters by Mr. Williamson. This Miri boasted that bis letters contained orders for the immediate despatch of troops to punish Rotung for the theft of some of Mr. Williamson’s rations. The dis- covery of this theft had been made at Rotung by Mr. Williamson during his maroh to Komsing and for it Mr. Williamson had said he would require satisfaction on his return. The hot*heads at Rotung immediately determined that the Miri should never reach the plains with the letters and, in accordance with this resolve, all four men wore murdcrod near Rcnging noxt morning. 11 By this murder, the party hostile to Mr. Williamson,

already strong, was considerably augmented and, urged on by the argument that, as punitive measures were certain to be attempted by the British for the murder of the Miri and the coolies, it was obviously the wisest course to slaughter all intruders who oould give, informa- tion either of the country or the events leading up to the massacre, the Eebang and Itotung men crossed the Dihang and killed all Mr. Williamson’s party, exoept 6 coolies who managed to effeot their escape. The seoond of the three periods is thus reached. The murder of Mr. Williamson naturally caused Operettas great ezoitement along the Frontier and many of our °“ r 1h# subjects living near the Pasi-Minyong border showed 1 r ’ signs of panic, which however was allayed by the prompt measures taken by the Deputy Commissioner, Lakhimpur, and the Commandant of the Military Polioe Battalion stationed at Dibrugarh. A force at once advanced to Pasighat, but no general advanoe was possible to Kebang and Komsing owing to the lateness of the season. A stockade however waB erected at Balek, a Pasi Abor village situated five miles from Pasighat, and commanding this group of five Pasi villages, and several expeditions against hostile Minyong villages wore oarried out successfully. The activities of this force effectually protected the Frontier from raids by the Abors till the Abor expedition was mobi- lized and oommenood its operations late in 1911. It had been decided that, on this occasion, no risks were to be run in dealing with Botung, Eebang and the other Minyong villages which were implicated in the massaore, and an exceedingly strong force under the eemmand of Major General Bower was despatched to execute the orders of the Government of India. These orders were : — (1) To exact severe punishment and reparation for the murder of Mr. Williamson and Dr. Gregorson and their party. 12 (2) To visit as many Minyong villages as possible, and make the tribe clearly understand that in future they would be under our control, which, subject to good behaviour on their part, would be of a loose political , nature. (8) To visit the Padam village of Damro. (4) . To explore and survey as much of the country as possible, visiting the Pemakoi falls, if prac- ticable, and incidentally settle the question of the identity of the Tsangpo and Brahmaputra

rivers. (5) To submit proposals for a suitable frontier line between India and Tibet. The opportunity was also taken to despatch three missions, up the Lohit, into the Miri country lying to the west of Subansiri river, and up the Dibong river, in order that (he work done, in the matter of the instructions oonveyod in items (4) and (6) above should be part of a comprehensive whole, and not merely an isolated achievement on a section of the Frontier. It <was hopod that as a result of these combined operations a complete and much-needed survey would be effected of the tumbled mass of inhospitable mountains whioh stretch from the plains of Assam to the main range of the Himalayas, the natural boundary of Tibet and Assam. Benin of Though the full results which were hoped for when tib* expdi- these orders issued were not realized, very valuable 4l0U *- work was done during the cold weather of 1611-12. The actual operations and achievements of the Abor expe- dition are matters of publio knowledge and it is sufficient to say that the expedition established our military superiority in the estimation of the Abor tribes generally and the Minyongs in particular, tbat.it con- firmed the friendliness of the Padams, whose chief village Damro, was visited, and that it accom- plished much useful survey and exploration work. Simultaneously, the three missions* mentioned above 13 achieved considerable success in surveying and bringing into closer touch the areas with whioh they were oalled upon to deal. At the end of the working season, it was decided Dot to leave all this valuable work unfi- nished and accordingly late in 1912 the Abcr survey commenced its operations. Linked with this, another survey 1 party was despatched to complete the mapping of the area drained by tbe Dibong river and its tributaries, surely some of the steepest country that exists. Two of the officers who accompanied this party crossed the Dibong-Dihang divide, in tbe vicinity or tho main Himalayan range, to tbe Upper Dihong valley and continued their explorations into Tibet. Thence they omerged into the Darrang district of Assam many months later, after a most adventurous journey which solved finally those muoh discussed geographical questions, the existence of the Tsangpo falls ana the identity of that river with the Dihong of Assam. The Abor survey party on their side succeeded in crossing

the Dos hung- La pass and reaching Fhea Doshung on the Tibet Bide of the main H imalayan range. On the return of these two parties, it was found that the desired suivey had, with the exooption of one or two unimport- ant areas, been completed throughout the mountains drained by the Dibong river and by the Dihong in its course south of the main range. Meanwhile, further east, the Walong promenade had visited Bima in Tibet, and the Mishmi work party and the Publio Works Department had commenced the construction of the Lonit Valley Road from Sadiya with a view to the open- ing up of communications in that direction. Another interesting tour was made during the cold weather of 1918-13 by an Assistant Political Officer through the country to the aouth of tbe Lohit stretching as far as the Turong river to the south and the Noa Dehing to the east. The people are ignorant and no concise accounts of symptoms in epidemics is ordinarily available, but influenza has lingered in the district since the universal epidemic of 1919, and sporadic oases arc reported. Vaccination is confined to the civi- lised portions of the district. Cholera occasionally occurs on tho southern banks of the Lohit, amongst tea-garden ooolies and iaati dwellers, but fortunately there has beon no large epidemic. Goitre is very common among the plains people and is found among hillmen except the Naga clans. Notwithstanding all theso ills, the health of the dis- trict is fairly good, and the mortality as reported not high. A high proportion of the deaths is amongst the pauper immigrants, who seem to think Sadiya an Eldorado and persist in coming to a township that is too needy in itself to support a floating oolony of beggars. Vital statistics are reported from the one mauza, tho one tea garden of the district, and from the Saw Mills areas at MurkoDg Selek and Laimekuri. The bulk of the district, however, does not report these occurences, so no ratio per mille oan be given to convey the rise and fall of the population. Bnt if occupancy returns oan supply a criterion, lhe*popu]ation is on the .increase, for considerable bodies of able-bodied Nepali ■settlers frequently arrive and undoubtedly, add to the number of births. The bulk of the people live

in huts of bamboo and thatch, and speedy deterioration necessitates the oonstruotion of new houses on new sites. Sinoe the material of the old houses is too decayed to use again, tbis occasional change of xvaidftnoe 41 combined with the advantages of chang houses oonduocs to a fair amount of oomfort, and by reducing tho ills arising from filth, gives the district a fairly clean bill of health. As already mentioned, there have been no regular £pidomio<. epidemics. Figures are reliable for the epidemic diseases of cholera and influenza, but only rolate to the administered portions of the district in which regular dispensaries are maintained. In all oases reported in time, Colonel Sir Leonard Roger's routine treatment has been adopted for oholera, while for influenza P. I. P. vaccine curative as well as preventive has been injeoted. The plains Abors, Mishmis, Khamtis and Singphoes suffered heavily in the great influenza epidemic of 1918. The two diseases cannot be said to be endemic in any particular looality and have undoubtedly been communioated by in footed persons arriving in the district. Other prevailing diseases in order of frequency are goitre, worms, malarial fevers and skin diseases. Kala azar has not been met with in the district but a curious blaok pigmentation of the skin, mostly of the face, has been observed in a few persons who though now perfectly well, say they suffered from fever when the pigmentation began. The appearanoe of the skin is as though damaged by gunpowder. Venereal diseases are fortunately rare, the few cases that occur being usually of persons infected outside the distriot. Mala- ria is on the increase, which is partly explained by the influx into the district of emigrants, already infected. Many of them arrive with enlarged spleens; the anopheles mosquito does the rest. No besbaruas are found among the Assamese popu- iaiigenou lotion, so these is no specific line of indigenous medical tmtment - treatment. Older folk, especially amongst the Ahom population, have oeriain remedies mostly of a herbal nature, but no ooaxing oan persuade them to give any particulars of the herbs used. There are however very 42 Forests. few persons that pretend to any knowledge of the cure of disease. Most of the villagers believe in charms, and present

votive offerings at the local shrines, the most celebrated being that of llalia Baba at Sadiya. Very little is known of their lino of indigenous treatment followed by the Mongolian tribes. The Khamtis are however reported to have ‘ vaids ’ who have some system of medicine of their own. It is quite possible too that tbe Mishmis who barter herbs and various portions of the wild animals at Sadiya, may have adopted the same as remedies for sickness amongst themselves, namely, musk’and the stomach of poroupine and hears. Bear’s stomach is bought by Chinese from Calcutta as a cure for dyspepsia and the root “ Mishmi Teeta ” is used as an infusion for malarial fever and a collyrium for sore eyes. There are indi- genous midwives practising their calling in tbe township of Sadiya but the bulk of the district’s women folk receive no expert assistance. The hill tribes have their “ Medioine Men, ” whoso methods are a combination of medicine and sorcery, the latter being usually the method that appeals to the afflicted person. The district being at present but sparsely populated the greater part is under so-called forest. No estimate of tbe area oan be given as tbe distriot has not yet been topographically surveyed. All waste land is techni- cally termed unolossod state forest : the stand varies from grass, reeds, and a swamp to a heavy timber, but the greater portion carries timber of some sort. The tree-Doaring portion is tvpioal mixed evergreen forest with dense undergrowth and ereeper covered trees. Over the greater portion the trees are very scattered ; standing singly or in groups, the intervening spaces being filled with masses of creeper or bamboos. Well stocked areas are generally of relatively small extent, bat on these very large trees are found. The predomi- nating species in the plains is “ Terminalia Myriocarpa” looally called ‘hollock’, but on the soath bank of the Brahmaputra or Lohit and along the Noa-Dehing river, Hollong, or '* Dipterocarpua Pilosus," becomes the 45 prevailing aperies over many areas. The foothills, as a rule, are oovered with heavier timber than the plains but of the same mixed evergreen type excent that Terminalia Myriooarpa does not predominate or aoes so very rarely. One timber reserve and seven fuel reserves aggregat- ing some 68 sq. miles were constituted in 1924 under the Assam Forest Regulation. In addition to these, eighty areas aggregating some 354 sq. miles are notified as Protected Forests by executive order of the

Political Officer. The names and areas of all the above will be found in the Appendix (page 58). The general control of all Government forests is Uanagmeat. vested in a Deputy or Assistant Conservator whose position is defined as that of advisor on forest matters to the Political Officer. The general rules in force for oontrol and exploitation in the other plains districts of Assam are followed exocpt in areas which the Political Officer oonsiderB unsuitable. All persons hold* ing land temporarily settled for cultivation are allowed to remove all forest produce needed for their own use free of any royalty. The largest Forest industry is the manufacture of tea boxes, and this is in the hands of the Assam Saw Mills and Timber Company, Limited, who have two Mills in the District. The more important of the two is the Veneor factory at Murkong Selek where three-ply boxes are manufactured from hardwood timber. For this work the species used at present exclusively is Hollook (Termi* nalia myriooarpa). The other mill is situated at Laime- kuri, and manufactures “ shooks ” from soft wood timber, the species most in demand being Simul (Bombax Mala- baricum). Formerly this species alone was used, but of late years supplies have beoome less accessible and several other aperies are utilised, the principal of which ase Piohola (Melioema Simplicifoiia), and Borpat (Allan- thus grandis). Each of these factories consumes daily, about 1,000 o. ft. of timber for working. 44 A lease £or a period of 30 years granting the sole right to exploit timber from the plains portion of the district (excluding Fuel Reserves) was granted in 1922 to the Assam Saw Mills and Timber Company. The greater part of the timber exploited by them is used for the manufacture of tea boxes in the Milh referred to above, but quantities of hardwoods are also exploited as scantlings. Apart from timber a substantial amount of the forest revenue of tho district is obtained from oane (calamus tennis), thatching grass, and from captured elephants. The thatching grass grows on chapris in the Brahmapu- tra and finds a ready sale in Dibrugarh. Both this and cane are disposed of as Mahals, the purchaser paying a considerable sum for the solo right to the produoo. No regular working plan has up to the present been prepared for any forest in the district, but there is a work- ing scheme since 1921 whereby an area sufficient to yield an amount of hardwood timber equal to the amount

exploited annually is regenerated artiS daily eaoh year. The annual coupe thus regenerated is a block of approxi- mately 80 acres. Timber The most frequent and commercially, the most valu- able tree is Hollock (Terminalia Myriocarpa) ; the next plaoe must at present be given to Simul (Bombax Malahftricum), followed by Hollong (Dipterocarpus Filosus) and Uriam (Bischofia J&vanica). Other trees valuable beoauso of the durable or other special qualities of their timber, though occurring spora- dically, arc Bola (Morus Laevigata), Gunseroi (Cinna- xnonum Glanduliferum and Cecicodaphne), Foma (Cedrcla febrifuga), Boga Poma or Silling (Chikrasia tabularis), Mekahi (Phoebe Hainesiana), Gomari fGmelina arborea), Sam (Artooarpus Chaplasa), Jutuli (Altingia Excelsa), Phulsona (Mangolia Spp.) and Tita- sopa (Mechelia Spp.). Toe Ohalmugra tree (Tarak- togenos Kurzii) also ooours in limited numbers. The most valuable tree so far found in the higher hills is the Walnut (Juglans Eegia). 45 There are 14 Government schools in the distriot, name- ly, one Middle English school and 18 Primary schools. The Middle English sohool which is located at Sadiya has shown a steady increase in the number of pupils in the roll. It has a staff of 5 teachers, and it is the only school in the distriot in whioh English is taught, pt the 13 Primary schools six are in Assamese, five in Miri, and two in Abor villages. Assameso is taught in all these schools. The schools in the Assamese villages have Assamese pandits while those in the Miri and Abor villages with one exception have Miri pandits. The Assamese village schools are all flourishing, but not so those of the Miri and Abor village schools, partly owing to the want of good Miri teachers, and partly to the apa- thy of boys and guardians alike. The people appear to be keen on having a school and evince much interest when one is started, but this interest is apt to die when the novelty wears off. 8adiya is the headquarters of the 2nd (Lakhimpur) Battalion of the Assam Rifles, for whom permanent barracks were constructed in 1920-21. The classes recruited are Gurkhas, Oacharis, Mech, Rava and Ahoms. The battalion furnishes the oordon of outposts on the Frontier. It is offioered by one Commandant and three Assistant Commandants, who are British officers of the Indian Army on deputation, by eight Subadars and nine Jemadars. The Battalion has a distinguished record

Tbe Sadiya Frontier Tract may be divided into foar different portions marked by special distinguishing geological features : — (a) The hill ranges north west and north of Sadiya, which form the eastern continuation of tbe Himalayas. ( b ) The hill ranges east of Brahmakund lying across the head of the Assam Valley. (e) The lower ranges of Manabum, Miaobum and the Patkois lying some distance south-east of Sadiya. The Sadiya Frontier Tract do^s not form an isolated geological unit and its pist history can be dcciphere l only by reference to other areas of which the geology is better known. A chapter on the u Past History of the Himalayan Area 99 is included in the Memoir by Colonel Bu'rrard and Sir Henry Hayden. 22. It seems likely that the old Metamorphic rocks were deposited on the bed of a considerable soa which covered most of what is now India. The subsequent history of the Frontier Tract is quite unknown until the much later GondwaUa period is reached ; at that time a large sea or ocean (known to geologists as the Tethys) occupied the present Tibet as well as other countries to the east and to the west. The southern shore of this sea

probably lay in a more or less east and west line passing through or near to the Saliya Frontier Tract and to the south lay a very large continent (known as Gondwana-land) extending over much of Australia, India, and Africa. There was considerable volcanic activity near the coast line of the old Tethys sea and the Abor basalts are lava flows from these old volcanoes ; it may be surmised that for a fairly long time there (existed in the northern part of the Gondwana-land marshy coastal plains which were covered with vegetation from which were derived the coal seems of Damuda age. 2d. After the period of deposition of these early coal-bearing rocks there is another great break in the history of the area but it can be surmised that most of the Frontier Tract continued as part of the continent of Gondwana-land. Just before the Tertiary period as a result of subsidences of the earth's crust this great continent began to break up and the sea commenced an advance in a north-cab terly direction towards Upper Assam, eventually submerging a great part, possibly all, of the present Sadiya Frontier Tract- A large area — including tbe present bites of the Himalayas, the Assam Valley and tbe Naga Hills— received a great thickness of shallow water deposits and during a long period this area was almost continously sinking. The deposits were probably derived from land to the north which was uplifted during the commencement of the folding movements which gave rise to the Himalayan ranges. During most of this period abundant vegetation grew in swampy areas within or bordering upon the gulf or estuary which had its head somewhere near the northern portion of the Sadiya Frontier Tract. Later in the Tertiary period the gulf became almost entirely silted up and the continua- tion of the mountain building movements resulted in the formation of the great hill ranges of tbe Himalayas and Pattern separated by a deep depression. Since their original uplift these ranges have been subjected to intense denudation. 89 24. The Sadiya Frontier Traot contains evidence of the very recent age of the great folding and mountain building movements that were responsible for the uplift of the Himalayas, Although the age of the Dihing Series oannot he nreouely ascertained, its occurronce at inclinations up to 85° ana 90° and the absence of evidence of widespread discordance amongst the various Tertiary rock series show that muoh of the folding must have taken place in very late Tertiary times. From the evidence of high level alluvial deposits and the steep gradient of such streims as the Dihang and Dibang it seoms likely that uplift is still in progress or has only quite recently ecasod. The Balipara Frontier Tract is bounded on the north ph y «ioai by Bhutan, Tibet and the hills inhabited by the Mombas upeoti. of Rupa and Shergaon, the Akas, Dallas, Apa Tanangs and Hill Mins ; on the west it is bonnded by the district of Kamrup and on the south and east by the districts of Darrang and Lakhimpur. From the plains there are a considerable number of passes into the hills, the principal being the TJdalguri- Amratulla trade route into Tibet ; this is actually the shortest route between India and Lhassa, the distanoe being 311 miles, against 350 by the Ohumbi Valley route. This road is good excepting for the first 25 mileB. Other passes weBt of the Bhoreli are the Doimara* Rupa and Doimara-Shergaon routes, and the Chard uar- Bfaalukpung route into the Aka Hills. The passes from Doimara are easy and practical for paok animals. East of the Bhoreli there are many routes leading into the hills. They are difficult and only fit for coolie transport. Many rivers drain the hills on this portion of the Frontier. The two largest are the Snbansiri and the Bhoreli, both of which break through the main snow range to the north .having their sources in the table

lands of Tibet. Wild animals which are found in the tract are wild Elephant, Rhinooeroe (both unioornis and Sumatrensis), anima1 *- Buffalo (Bos bubaHs) Bison or Mithon (Bos gaurus and Bos frontalis). Of deer, are found the Sambh&r, Hog deer„Ohital, Swamp, Musk, and Barking deer. Of goats, the Serow and Gurral, and in the further hills the Takin (Budoroas taxicolor). The tiger, leopard, olouoed leopard, sloth bear, binturong, pig, pigmy hog, the wild dog, and many kinds of oats. i History. Inhabitants. Mombas. The southern portion of the tract originally formed part of the districts of Darrang and Lakhimpur and the early history of this portion ■will be found iu the Gazetteer of these districts. In 1914, the Western Section, North-East Frontier, was formed into a district under the control of a Political Offioer. Monyiil meaning in Tibetan “ lhe low country ” is a name applied to the portion of the North-East Fron- tier about 2,000 square miles in extent, which is wedged in between Bhutan on the west and the Miji and Aka Hills on the east. It is divided from Tibet proper by a wild range of mountains averaging 16,000 feet. The people inhabiting this area are called by the Tibetans Mombas, i e , inhabitants of the Monytil (low country). The inhabitants of the triangle south of the Sela Range are divided loosely into two main tribes, viz., Sherchokpa and Sherdukpen. The Sherchokpa live in the valley of the Dirang Chu as far as the village of Rahung and of the Nagum Chu (Dhansiri river) ; the Sherdukpen are the inhabi- tants of the villages of Shergaon and Rupa. The Mombas north of the Sela are under the admini- stration of the Tsonajong Jongpens one of whom is a monk, the other a layman, appointed by the authorities at Lhassa. In the summer time these two officials live at Tsonajong, in Tibet proper; in the winter time they live at Tawang in the Monyiil. Tsonajong is a place of some importance as a trade mart, as here the Assam Trade route is intersected by the Trade route from Eastern Tibet and China. All revenues collected by the Tsana Jongpens are sent direct to Lhassa. South of the Sela, the Sheroholcpas are under

the oontrol of two monk Jongpens appointed by the tawang monastery, a large monastery of 500 monks, an 8 offshoot of the important Drepung monastery at Lhaisa with the exception, of the village of Senge Dzong which is under the Tsona Jongpens. All revenues collected by the monk Jongpens go to the support of the monastery. The language spoken varies greatly from village to village, but the majority speak a dialect resembling the language spoken in Eastern Bhutan. These Mombas are a quiet law ^ abiding people amongst whom serious crime is practically unknown, they are excellent farmers, industrious and hard work- ing, and if it were not for the exactions levied by the monks the country would be very prosperous. The dress of the Momba is distinctive ; he wears a short coarse woollen Ohuba or Tibetan .Cloak dyed red, which reaches a short way below the hips ; underneath he wears short loose pants of coarse white cotton cloth. Sis hair is cut short just above the eyes and at the nape of the neck, and on his head he wears a peculiar dome shaped cap of Yak hair with untrimmed edges. In his belt he invariably carries a short Btout sword in a wooden scabbard. The Jongpens of Tsona receive annually a subsidy of B.s. 5,000 from the British Government under Treaty (see Aitchison’s Treaties, Part IV, Bhutan No. OVx, Page 267). Of this amount Rs. 500 is kept by the Tawang monastery, and the balance sent to the Drepung monastery at JLihassa. The Sh er duk pen are a small tribe of Mombas, in- dependent of Tawang, and live in the large villages of Shergaon and Rupa. These two villages were formerly called Ruprai Gya and Bur Gya, but from con- stant dealings with Assam the present form has been adopted. They are auiet peace loving agriculturists and are finer men than the other Mombas living south of the Bela. These two villages are ruled by a joint council of seven headmen, who in the old days were. called 8&t JELajh by the Assamese. These people are divided into two classes, the upper or the hereditary land holders and a poorer class called Giba. Them is no slavery amongst them. They mix little with other Mombas. They migrate to the Plains at Doimara in the Frontier Tracts for fire months every year, and bring with them all their live stock consisting of ponies, mules and a very fine handsome breed of cattle.

They received from us a yearly subsidy of Es. 2,526* 7*0, and oonsider themselves under the protection of the British Eaj. The Tembang, Konia and But Mombas were called in the past “ the Thebengia Bhufcias ” by the Assamese. This year was the year of the Oaleutta Exhibition, and specimens of agricultural inplements and products, wearing apparel, ornaments rand weapons of Frontier tribes were wanted for exhibit. It was deoided to send an Expedition and a mixed foroe of 970 men including two mountain guns entered the Aka hills in the cold weather of 1884. The advance guard of 150 men was attacked and held up at Tonga river and two men were killed and seven wounded ; the main body then came up, the passage of the river was foroed, the Akas retreated and tne Kovat- sun village was occupied ; the Akas however retired from their villages and hid themselves in the jungle. This distriot consists of terai and hill tracts, both sparsely populated. The terai is unhealthy like all other tracts lying under the hills in Assam. Fever is prevalent and kala agar has appeared. The Sadiya Frontier Tract is the North-East Front- in* and ier Distriot of India, bordering on Tibet on the north bouadana*. and east and on Bnrma on the south and south-east. The Distriot was formed in 1912 with headquarters at Sadiya and with the old Sadiya Subdivision of the Lakhimpur Distriot as a nucleus, under the name “ Central and Eastern Seothms, North-East Frontier," whioh was later ehanged to the present designation. It lies between 27 ° 15 ' and 29° north latitude and 94° 15 " and 97° east longitude, extending from the Subansiri river on the west to the Lohit-Brahmaputra-Irra- wady watershed. It includes the mountains on the southern faoe of the main Himalayan Divide, the west- ern and north-western slopes of the Dapha and Fhunkan ranges, which separate India from the extreme north of Burma and crosses the Patkoi Range to touoh the northern end of tho Hawkong Valley and run with the eastern portion of the unadministered area of the Naga Hills. Exoept where the distriot touches Lakhimpur, i.e., on the south, its boundaries have not

been . demarcated, following mainly as they do the principal ridges of tumbled masses of mountains, whioh form the eastern extremity of the Himalayan system. The area of the Tract is some 10,000 square miles, of whioh 3,500 square miles are under regular administra- tion. The latter area represents the plains and foot hills. The boundaries officially notified are as follows : — “ From Siplumukh on the Subansiri east along the ridge of the outer range to the Jiya Dhol river ; thsnoe down the right bank of the Jiya Dhol river to where it eats the Rajgarh Ali ; thence east along the foot of the bills following the village path running along the foot of the hills so as to include all Galong villages to the Dipa (8inyang) N.» east-south-east of Dipa village; thence down the right bank of the Dipa (Sinyang) N. to its confluence with the Si men river ; CHAPTER III. ARCHAEOLOGY AND TRADITIONS. Early hi»- To render intelligible an account of the ruins and tory, remains to be found within the Sadiya Frontier Tract, it is necessary first to give a brief outline of the early history of its inhabitants so far as this is known. There are no records or traditions available prior to the advent of Chutiyas whose Buranji gives the first recorded men- tion of Sadiya. The Chutiyas are believed to have been members of the great Bodo raoe, to have come from the north-east, and to have lived in large independent com- munities like the Nagas and Abors of the present day. There is a tradition, however, that the Chutiyas origi- nally came down the Bubansiri valley, and that one Bibar, a local chief, attained a measure of supremacy over the other villages. This position was improved by his son, who called himself ‘ Lord of the Hills ’ and descended the Brahmaputra valley, where he defeated Bhadra Sen and founded a capital at Ratnapura on the Majuli, or in North Lakhimpur. Gaur was at that time under Hindu dynasty, so the Ohutiya eruption must have been previous to 1204A.D. The Chutiya leader, assumed the name of Ratnadwaj Pal, exca- vated tanks, constructed forts, etc., and there are to-day within seven miles of modern Sadiya large tanks . with brioked sides whioh are believed to have been originally exoavated by the Chutiyas. The remains of forts at the foot of the hills, at Bishemnagar and at other places, are probably traceable to the same times. Bat ir

17 nadwag is said to hare visited Gaur and on his return left a son there to be educated. The boy died and the body was sent back to the father, who reoeived it when he was building a new city. The Ahom reoords show that when they entered Assam in 1228 A.D. the Ohutiyas were established at Badiya and were masters of the country westwards as far as the Disang river. Hostilities broke out about the middle of the 14th oentury, and in 1528 (or according to the Chutiya chronioles about 1673 A. D.) the Ahoms finally defeated the Ohutiyas at Ohantam or Ohandangiri. There are said to have been four subdivisions among the Ohutiyas, namely, Hindu. Ahom, Deori and Borahi. The Deoris are the old priestly caste, attendants on the gods, and possibly the class from whom tbe annual B&crifioo was at one time chosen. Apart from timber a substantial amount of the forest revenue of tho district is obtained from oane (calamus tennis), thatching grass, and from captured elephants. The thatching grass grows on chapris in the Brahmapu- tra and finds a ready sale in Dibrugarh. Both this and cane are disposed of as Mahals, the purchaser paying a considerable sum for the solo right to the produoo. No regular working plan has up to the present been prepared for any forest in the district, but there is a work- ing scheme since 1921 whereby an area sufficient to yield an amount of hardwood timber equal to the amount

exploited annually is regenerated artiS daily eaoh year. The annual coupe thus regenerated is a block of approxi- mately 80 acres. Timber The most frequent and commercially, the most valu- able tree is Hollock (Terminalia Myriocarpa) ; the next plaoe must at present be given to Simul (Bombax Malahftricum), followed by Hollong (Dipterocarpus Filosus) and Uriam (Bischofia J&vanica). Other trees valuable beoauso of the durable or other special qualities of their timber, though occurring spora- dically, arc Bola (Morus Laevigata), Gunseroi (Cinna- xnonum Glanduliferum and Cecicodaphne), Foma (Cedrcla febrifuga), Boga Poma or Silling (Chikrasia tabularis), Mekahi (Phoebe Hainesiana), Gomari fGmelina arborea), Sam (Artooarpus Chaplasa), Jutuli (Altingia Excelsa), Phulsona (Mangolia Spp.) and Tita- sopa (Mechelia Spp.). Toe Ohalmugra tree (Tarak- togenos Kurzii) also ooours in limited numbers. The most valuable tree so far found in the higher hills is the Walnut (Juglans Eegia). 45 There are 14 Government schools in the distriot, name- ly, one Middle English school and 18 Primary schools. The Middle English sohool which is located at Sadiya has shown a steady increase in the number of pupils in the roll. It has a staff of 5 teachers, and it is the only school in the distriot in whioh English is taught, pt the 13 Primary schools six are in Assamese, five in Miri, and two in Abor villages. Assameso is taught in all these schools. The schools in the Assamese villages have Assamese pandits while those in the Miri and Abor villages with one exception have Miri pandits. The Assamese village schools are all flourishing, but not so those of the Miri and Abor village schools, partly owing to the want of good Miri teachers, and partly to the apa- thy of boys and guardians alike. The people appear to be keen on having a school and evince much interest when one is started, but this interest is apt to die when the novelty wears off. 8adiya is the headquarters of the 2nd (Lakhimpur) Battalion of the Assam Rifles, for whom permanent barracks were constructed in 1920-21. The classes recruited are Gurkhas, Oacharis, Mech, Rava and Ahoms. The battalion furnishes the oordon of outposts on the Frontier. It is offioered by one Commandant and three Assistant Commandants, who are British officers of the Indian Army on deputation, by eight Subadars and nine Jemadars. Tbe Sadiya Frontier Tract may be divided into foar different portions marked by special distinguishing geological features : — (a) The hill ranges north west and north of Sadiya, which form the eastern continuation of tbe Himalayas. ( b ) The hill ranges east of Brahmakund lying across the head of the Assam Valley. (e) The lower ranges of Manabum, Miaobum and the Patkois lying some distance south-east of Sadiya. (<f) The large alluvial plain of the Brahmaputra and its tributaries, of which Sadiya is approximately the centra] point. 2. Although these areas are best described separately, it will be convenijnt 6 rat to consider the general sequence of strata in tbe district. The rooks composing the various ranges of hills differ greatly in geological age ; one large group (known as the Archean) is of very great geological antiquity, whilst another large group is almost the youngest of the big geological deposits. Represen- tatives of intermediate ages are albo found, but these cover a much smaller area. STRATIGRAPHY. 3. The rooks may be classified as follows : — V. Recent ••• ... River alluvium. IV. (Probably) Pleistocene ... Ill, Tertiary (Eocene to Pliocene). II. Gondwana (Permo-Carbo- niferous, etc.). I. Metamorphio (P re- Cam- brian). Older alluvial deposits. r Dihing Seiies. Tipam „ Coal Measure „ ^Disang „ Damuda Series, etc. Various rooks of great geological age. 4. The oldest rocks are sohists, {gneisses, quartzites, slates and

limestones. Comparatively little is known abont them, bat it is fairly certain that many, if not all, of these rooks are of Archean 83 or Pre-Cambrian age— i.e., they belong to the oldest known geolo- gical system, and are equivalent to rooks found elsewhere through out a largo part of India. 5. The rocks which immediately follow in the geological scale ^ age are not known to occur in the Frontior Tracts and the next system represented is the mueh newer Gondwana system. Rocks of this age ocour in large areas in Bengal and elsewhere, and amongst them are included the coal seams of the largo Indian coalfields. In the Sadiya Frontier Tract, however, the rocks arc mostly sandstones, quartsites, and shales, with but little coal. In the Abor country a great thickness of volcanic rooks are found inter- spersed in this scries ; of these rocks the most common are basaltic lavas, but volcanic “ ashes 99 (i.e-, tuffs) are also found. . The rocks have been correlated with the Damuda series — which is the subdivision of the Lower Gondwanas containing the actual workable seams of the Bengal coalfields. From the evidence of boulders containing marine fossils found in the Sabansiri river it appears that also the Lower Productus Limestone occurs somewhere in the hills. 6. Above the Gondwana beds there occurs another break in the geological sequence, and the next strata are of Tertiary age. The Tertiary rooks have been investigated in more detail than the older beds, and have been subdivided into a number of series and groups : — (a) Of the four different series the Disang Series, named after a river in the hills south-west of the Sadiya Frontier Tract, is the oldest, and possibly includes some^ beds of Cretaceous age as well as Lower Tertiary rocks (Eocene Oligocene). The Disang series is made up of many thousands of fe.t of grej shale with intorbedded flaggy sandstones, sandy shales and thin impure limestones. (fl) The "Disang rocks grade into a series of sandstones, shales, mudstone 3, etc., which is termed the Coal Measure. Series. This series is probably over 1<>,0 >0 feet thick and in it there occur many thin bods of co»l avid car- bonaceous shale. Except in the lower part of the series mottled and blue clays are common ; in the upper part there occurs in addition to the thin coals already men- tioned a group of fairly thick coal seams, which is traceable for a considerable distance in the Frontier Tracts and in the neighbouring portion of tbo Lakhim- pur district. In this Tatter district the seams are exten- sively worked in the various collieries of the Assam Railway and Trading Company and it was the occur- rence of these seams that led to the series receiving ite

name. 84 M Over the Coal Measures occurs the Tipam Series, so named from the Tipam hills near Jaipur (Lakhiiapur). This scries is also rather over 10,000 feet in thickness and has been sul>dividcd into three approximately equal portions ; the lowest consists of hard, false-bedded coarse, ferruginous, blue sandstones weathering to yellow, reddish and brown, with occasional bauds of mottled and blue clay. Above this group lies a succession of mottled clays, blue clays, sandy clays and clayey sand- stones with a few considerable beds of hard ferruginous sandstone. Above these clays lies a group of softer blue sandstones containing many fragments of lignite and pebbles of coal and lignite. (d) The most recent of the Tertiary divisions is the Dihing Scries, consisting of several thousand feet of pebble beds with subordinate bands of soft clay and sand- stone. 7. Above the Tertiary Series are the gravels, sands, and elay forming an “older" alluvium which was laid down when the rivers ran at a much g router elevation than they now do. Some of these bods occur as much as 1,000 feet above the present streams. Lastl) , there arc the pebble banks, sands and Bandy clayB now hoiug deposited iu the lower reaches of the numerous streams. 8. Correlation of the Tertiary rochs .— One of the most remark- able features of the thousands of feet of Assam Tertiaries is the almost complete absence of fossils. The only Tertiary fossils known in the Frontier Tracts are badly preserved leaf impressions and fragments of fossil wood. It is therefore from lithological comparisons with other areas that it is concluded that the Disang Sor es is mainly Lower Tertiary, that the Coal Measure and Tipam Scries are Middle Tertiary, and that the Dihing Series is Upper Tertiary. The total thickness of Tertiary rooks exceeds 30,000 feel and may bo as much as 40,000 feet. STRUCTURAL FEATURES. 9. Having reviewed the sequence of strata found in the Sadiya Frontier Tracts, it is now convenient to consider the cha- racteristics of tho four areas mentioned above. (a) The Bill Country North-West and North of Baity a, lp. The eastern continuation of the Himalayas, inhabited by tho Mirisj Abort, Mishmie, etc., has been very little examined by 85 geologists i the available geological information regarding tbU part of the area comes from the work done by the Geological Survey of In lia Maolaren in Volume XXXI oC the Record* of the Geological Survey of India writes “ These ranges are, without exception, inhabited by wild hill tribes, whose oi»ea or covert

hostility, Eupcradded to tho difficu’ty of obtaining transport and the natnral inhospitality of the mountains, mako^ a journey into them a matter of great difficulty if not of actual danger. Indeed our limited knowledge of the geology of their interior has boon mainly obtained during the progress of punitive expeditions 11, Those hills have a general wost-south-west, cast-north- east trend and the rooks found therein strike in the same general direction. The newest rocks occur along the south-eastern margin of the hills and progressively older rocks are found in a north- westerly direction. Throughout the ar.a the first bolt of rocks consists of steeply dipping sandstones and conglomerates of Ter- tiary age which have not been investigated in detail, but which doubtless belong to the Tipam and Dibiug Series. Such Tertiary rocks occur in a long belt throughout the Himalayas and they are well-known farther west as the Siwalik Series North-west of and parallel to the Tertiary rocks there is a narrow belt of tho Gondwana Series. These rocks have been greatly crushed by the various movements of the earth’s crust which have resulted in the uplift of the Himalayas and in oonsoquencc the coal is now found only in very badly crushed lentioles instead of in continuous seams. The series as a whole dips at a high inclination towards the north- west but there are many local variations due to the complications of the folding movements. Still further north-west lies a very great thickness of the metamorphic rocks. Topography .— Although the hills are not comparable in height to those of the two ranges already mentioned, the Tertiary outcrop includes areas of very considerable relief , and it is notice- able that tbc various rook groups Lave an important bearing on the topography of the country. The more shaly portions of the Disang Series usually occupy low ground but the harder flaggy sandstones stand out as prominent hill ranges. The Coal Measure Series generally occupies comparatively high ground although, owing to the complicated structure of the Coal Measure area9>well defined ridges are seldom noticeable. The sandstones in the lowest portion of the Tipam Series form very prominent hill ranges ; small streams crossing the outcrop have to cut their way through the hard sandstones and this usually results in a considerable series of waterfalls and ravines. In the larger streams these sandstones invariably form gorges with steep sides and deep pools. The over- lying clays give rise to comparatively low-lying country, which from the neighbouring sandstone ranges appears nearly flat, but which is nevertheless greatly broken by low steep ridges caused by the superior resistance of the sandstone beds to weathering. The sandstones forming the uppermost part of the Tipam Series are comparatively soft but occur in hills of .considerable height between Manabum and the Dihing. The outcrop of the Dihing Series is generally marked by low broken hills in which cliffs formed by the pebble bods are common. 16. Structure . — The outcrop of Tertiary rooks may, from a structural point of view, be divided into three portions. 17. (0 The Fatkai range is a scarp of various sandstone beds near the base of the Coal Measures and in the Disang Series, and throughout a large area near the Patkais the rooks have a general west-south-west, east-north-east strike. The Nonryong Valley on the south side of the Patkais is occupied by a synoline iu Coal Measures, The broken ground immediately to the north of the Patkais including the Honkapbum and Nunnunbum ranges and extending north-east to the confluence of the Nam Dapha contains rocks of all the Tertiary divisions except the Dihings 87 and the structure although conforming in general to the west soutb* west, east-north-east trend, is decidedly complex. A series of strike faults have been identified running approximately parallel to the Patkai range. These faults are accompanied by a consi- derable amount of contortion specially in the Disang and Coal Measure Series and this line of disturbance represents the conti- nuation of the Disang Thrust Fau’t of the Naga Hills. The rocks dip at very high angles, being u&uilly vertical or somewhat invert- ed and their strike, although variable, is more or loss parallel to the Patkais. 18. (it) The rooks occurring in the hills to the north-ea6t of

the Noa Dihing ((-he Manabum Range) and in the upper reaches of the Nam Dapha do not show any signs of the west-south-west, east-north-east structural lines, but have a north-north-west, south-south-east strike which is nearly parallel to the direction of folding bhown in the Miju and other ranges east of Brahmaknnd. In the area from the Tenga Pani to the Noa Dihing the lower divisions of the Tertiary rooks lie at a considerable depth below the surface and only the Dihing Series and the uppermost part of the Tipam Series are to be found outcropping. 19. (ffV) Besides these two areas in which the structure oon* forms to well marked lines of folding, there is an intervening area including most of the Miaobum range where the rooks have felt the effeot of both systems of folding and accordingly exhibit most com- plex structure. In this area oocur both Coal Measures and Tipams, but the dips vary from horizontal to vertical and conform to no general direction, and it is evident that the rooks have been severely folded and also considerably faulted. (d) Low ground near Sadiya . 20. The remaining portion of the Sadiya Frontier Tract is the low ground bordering the Dihang, Dibang, Lohit and Noa Dihing rivers. This stretch of oountry is entirely composed of alluvial deposits brought down from the hills by tbe large rivers. This alluvium forms a complete mask entirely concealing the geological structure but we may surmise that there is a large synclinal area between the opposing lines of uplift of the Patkais and the Himalayas. It is believed that the alluvium readies a vast thick- ness probably measurable in thousands of feet, occupying a depression which has been slowly growing in depth ever since the time of the great Himalayan earth movements, a growth which is probably still continuing. The high level terraces of river gravel, already mentioned as occurring at heights up to as much as one thousand feet above tbe level of the valley, are found near the bead of tbe Diyun (Dihing), and near Nieamghat on the Dibang and Pasighat on tbe Dihaug. 88 GEOLOGICAL HISTORY. 21. The Sadiya Frontier Tract do^s not form an isolated geological unit and its pist history can be dcciphere l only by reference to other areas of which the geology is better known. A chapter on the u Past History of the Himalayan Area 99 is included in the Memoir by Colonel Bu'rrard and Sir Henry Hayden. 22. It seems likely that the old Metamorphic rocks were deposited on the bed of a considerable soa which covered most of what is now India. The subsequent history of the Frontier Tract is quite unknown until the much later GondwaUa period is reached ; at that time a large sea or ocean (known to geologists as the Tethys) occupied the present Tibet as well as other countries to the east and to the west. The southern shore of this sea

probably lay in a more or less east and west line passing through or near to the Saliya Frontier Tract and to the south lay a very large continent (known as Gondwana-land) extending over much of Australia, India, and Africa. There was considerable volcanic activity near the coast line of the old Tethys sea and the Abor basalts are lava flows from these old volcanoes ; it may be surmised that for a fairly long time there (existed in the northern part of the Gondwana-land marshy coastal plains which were covered with vegetation from which were derived the coal seems of Damuda age. 2d. After the period of deposition of these early coal-bearing rocks there is another great break in the history of the area but it can be surmised that most of the Frontier Tract continued as part of the continent of Gondwana-land. Just before the Tertiary period as a result of subsidences of the earth's crust this great continent began to break up and the sea commenced an advance in a north-cab terly direction towards Upper Assam, eventually submerging a great part, possibly all, of the present Sadiya Frontier Tract- A large area — including tbe present bites of the Himalayas, the Assam Valley and tbe Naga Hills— received a great thickness of shallow water deposits and during a long period this area was almost continously sinking. The deposits were probably derived from land to the north which was uplifted during the commencement of the folding movements which gave rise to the Himalayan ranges. During most of this period abundant vegetation grew in swampy areas within or bordering upon the gulf or estuary which had its head somewhere near the northern portion of the Sadiya Frontier Tract. Later in the Tertiary period the gulf became almost entirely silted up and the continua- tion of the mountain building movements resulted in the formation of the great hill ranges of tbe Himalayas and Pattern separated by a deep depression. Since their original uplift these ranges have been subjected to intense denudation. 89 24. The Sadiya Frontier Traot contains evidence of the very recent age of the great folding and mountain building movements that were responsible for the uplift of the Himalayas, Although the age of the Dihing Series oannot he nreouely ascertained, its occurronce at inclinations up to 85° ana 90° and the absence of evidence of widespread discordance amongst the various Tertiary rock series show that muoh of the folding must have taken place in very late Tertiary times. From the evidence of high level alluvial deposits and the steep gradient of such streims as the Dihang and Dibang it seoms likely that uplift is still in progress or has only quite recently ecasod. ECONOMIC GEOLOGY. 25. Coal.— Coal occurs in two separate Geological Series. The older (Gondwana) coal has been so badly crushed by the

mountain building movements that the outcrops in the Frontier Tracts have no commercial value. The newer coal seams arc found in the upper portion of the Coal Me j sure Series of the Tertiary and these are being worked in the adjacent Lakhimpur district. The seams in the Frontier Tracts are, however, much thinner ; they outcrop in the Miaobum and Nuanunl>um Ranges, but are fouud dipping at very high angles (80° for example) and are somewhat crushed and faulted. It does not seem at all likely that coal could at present be successfully extracted on a commercial scale. 26. 0f7.-»-Oil is obtained on a commeroial scale from the Tertiary rocks in the neighbouring Lakhimpur district and there is evidence of oil and gas in the Dihing Valley and the Nunnun- bura range associated with rockB of tho Coal Measure Series. Owing to the steeply folded and greatly faulted condition of the strata there seems no possibility whatever of any appreciable accummulation of oil having taken place and no areas have been found sufficiently promising for even a trial boring. 27. This gold is presumably obtained from gold-bearing quartz veins oecurring amongst the met^morphio rooks somewhere in the hills, but the locality is quite unknown. 28.
