The Balipara Frontier Tract is bounded on the north ph y «ioai by Bhutan, Tibet and the hills inhabited by the Mombas upeoti. of Rupa and Shergaon, the Akas, Dallas, Apa Tanangs and Hill Mins ; on the west it is bonnded by the district of Kamrup and on the south and east by the districts of Darrang and Lakhimpur. From the plains there are a considerable number of passes into the hills, the principal being the TJdalguri- Amratulla trade route into Tibet ; this is actually the shortest route between India and Lhassa, the distanoe being 311 miles, against 350 by the Ohumbi Valley route. This road is good excepting for the first 25 mileB. Other passes weBt of the Bhoreli are the Doimara* Rupa and Doimara-Shergaon routes, and the Chard uar- Bfaalukpung route into the Aka Hills. The passes from Doimara are easy and practical for paok animals. East of the Bhoreli there are many routes leading into the hills. They are difficult and only fit for coolie transport. Many rivers drain the hills on this portion of the Frontier. The two largest are the Snbansiri and the Bhoreli, both of which break through the main snow range to the north .having their sources in the table

lands of Tibet. Wild animals which are found in the tract are wild Elephant, Rhinooeroe (both unioornis and Sumatrensis), anima1 *- Buffalo (Bos bubaHs) Bison or Mithon (Bos gaurus and Bos frontalis). Of deer, are found the Sambh&r, Hog deer„Ohital, Swamp, Musk, and Barking deer. Of goats, the Serow and Gurral, and in the further hills the Takin (Budoroas taxicolor). The tiger, leopard, olouoed leopard, sloth bear, binturong, pig, pigmy hog, the wild dog, and many kinds of oats. i History. Inhabitants. Mombas. The southern portion of the tract originally formed part of the districts of Darrang and Lakhimpur and the early history of this portion ■will be found iu the Gazetteer of these districts. In 1914, the Western Section, North-East Frontier, was formed into a district under the control of a Political Offioer. Monyiil meaning in Tibetan “ lhe low country ” is a name applied to the portion of the North-East Fron- tier about 2,000 square miles in extent, which is wedged in between Bhutan on the west and the Miji and Aka Hills on the east. It is divided from Tibet proper by a wild range of mountains averaging 16,000 feet. The people inhabiting this area are called by the Tibetans Mombas, i e , inhabitants of the Monytil (low country). The inhabitants of the triangle south of the Sela Range are divided loosely into two main tribes, viz., Sherchokpa and Sherdukpen. The Sherchokpa live in the valley of the Dirang Chu as far as the village of Rahung and of the Nagum Chu (Dhansiri river) ; the Sherdukpen are the inhabi- tants of the villages of Shergaon and Rupa. The Mombas north of the Sela are under the admini- stration of the Tsonajong Jongpens one of whom is a monk, the other a layman, appointed by the authorities at Lhassa. In the summer time these two officials live at Tsonajong, in Tibet proper; in the winter time they live at Tawang in the Monyiil. Tsonajong is a place of some importance as a trade mart, as here the Assam Trade route is intersected by the Trade route from Eastern Tibet and China. All revenues collected by the Tsana Jongpens are sent direct to Lhassa. South of the Sela, the Sheroholcpas are under

the oontrol of two monk Jongpens appointed by the tawang monastery, a large monastery of 500 monks, an 8 offshoot of the important Drepung monastery at Lhaisa with the exception, of the village of Senge Dzong which is under the Tsona Jongpens. All revenues collected by the monk Jongpens go to the support of the monastery. The language spoken varies greatly from village to village, but the majority speak a dialect resembling the language spoken in Eastern Bhutan. These Mombas are a quiet law ^ abiding people amongst whom serious crime is practically unknown, they are excellent farmers, industrious and hard work- ing, and if it were not for the exactions levied by the monks the country would be very prosperous. The dress of the Momba is distinctive ; he wears a short coarse woollen Ohuba or Tibetan .Cloak dyed red, which reaches a short way below the hips ; underneath he wears short loose pants of coarse white cotton cloth. Sis hair is cut short just above the eyes and at the nape of the neck, and on his head he wears a peculiar dome shaped cap of Yak hair with untrimmed edges. In his belt he invariably carries a short Btout sword in a wooden scabbard. The Jongpens of Tsona receive annually a subsidy of B.s. 5,000 from the British Government under Treaty (see Aitchison’s Treaties, Part IV, Bhutan No. OVx, Page 267). Of this amount Rs. 500 is kept by the Tawang monastery, and the balance sent to the Drepung monastery at JLihassa. The Sh er duk pen are a small tribe of Mombas, in- dependent of Tawang, and live in the large villages of Shergaon and Rupa. These two villages were formerly called Ruprai Gya and Bur Gya, but from con- stant dealings with Assam the present form has been adopted. They are auiet peace loving agriculturists and are finer men than the other Mombas living south of the Bela. These two villages are ruled by a joint council of seven headmen, who in the old days were. called 8&t JELajh by the Assamese. These people are divided into two classes, the upper or the hereditary land holders and a poorer class called Giba. Them is no slavery amongst them. They mix little with other Mombas. They migrate to the Plains at Doimara in the Frontier Tracts for fire months every year, and bring with them all their live stock consisting of ponies, mules and a very fine handsome breed of cattle.

They received from us a yearly subsidy of Es. 2,526* 7*0, and oonsider themselves under the protection of the British Eaj. The Tembang, Konia and But Mombas were called in the past “ the Thebengia Bhufcias ” by the Assamese. Their villages are situated about 25 miles north of Rupa, on a fertile undulating plateau at an altitude of 6,000 feet ; they are a miserable, degraded people, being araoh ground down by the Mijis who are their immediate neighbours. la write of this they are hard working and if only they could obtain some measure of protection might become a prosperous community. These villages are independent of Tawang. They receive from us annually the sum of Es. 145*16-6 as Posa. The Mombas are Buddhists and in most of their villages is a Gompa (temple) and to judge from outward signs they should do good Buddhists for on every corner of the road one finds a " Mane ” wall or Chorten and in the neighbourhood of eaoh village every stream is used to turn a huge prayer wheel. Their Buddhism, however, is very superficial ; in the few villages that have priests these have sucoumbed to the world the flesh and the devil and taken unto themselves wives thus ipw facto renouncing their holy orders. They however continue to perform their office though they have long lost the respect of their flocks. Th« Aku. The Akas inhabit the Tonga, Bigien, and lower part of the Biohom river valleys. The word 'Aka* means in Assamese painted, the Tibetan name for these people is Kh&nonh or Black lips, both names are doe to the Aka habit of smearing 5 their lips and cheeks with a black xesinom substanoe dorived from the Blue pine (Pinas Sxcelta) ns a pro- tection against biting flies and blistering winds. The Akas call themselves Hruaso. They claim desoent from two ohiefs, Notapur and Bayu, who in anoient times lived in the stone forts at Bhalukpung on the Bhoreli river. The remains of these forts are still to he seen. Though a small tribe the Akas are superior in edu- cation and civilization to their neighbours and are held in high esteem by them. Praotioally nothing is known of the history of the Their w»to- Akas before the British occupation. The British first ry - came in oont&et with the tribe in 1829 when the depre- dations of Tagi, the Kovatsun chief, necessitated notion being taken against them. Tagi was arrested and

confined for four yean in the Gauhati Gaol. Imme- diately on release he took again to his old habits of raiding whioh culminated in the oaipture and massaore of a small military outpost at Balipara in 1885. A price was placed on his head but no expedition was made into the Hills. r In 1841 he twioe raided and carried off British subjects into the hills. On this the Government half-heartedly gave sanction for an expe- dition against him, but whilst preparations were being made he came in and surrendered. He was forgiven, on condition of his swearing allegiance and a pension of Bs. 240 was bestowed on him, in 1844 this pension was increased to Bs. 860 per annum and agam was increased to Bs. 520 in 1848. The Akas gave no farther trouble until 1888. This year was the year of the Oaleutta Exhibition, and specimens of agricultural inplements and products, wearing apparel, ornaments rand weapons of Frontier tribes were wanted for exhibit. The Mauzadar of Balipara was sent up with 18 followers by the Govern- . ment to try to procure these articles, and if possible to obtain an Aka man and woman for the purpose of modelling. The request was made in a manner that so 6 Organisa- tion. inoensed the Aka Chief that he seized the Mauzadar and his servant and oonfined them, but allowed the other 12 to go free. At the same time the KutBon chief Medhi, raided the Forest Outpost near Balipara and carried off a Banger and Clerk. It was deoided to send an Expedition and a mixed foroe of 970 men including two mountain guns entered the Aka hills in the cold weather of 1884. The advance guard of 150 men was attacked and held up at Tonga river and two men were killed and seven wounded ; the main body then came up, the passage of the river was foroed, the Akas retreated and tne Kovat- sun village was occupied ; the Akas however retired from their villages and hid themselves in the jungle. When with great difficulty communications were esta- blished, it was learned that the mauzadar was dead ; the two forest officials were released and some muskets and bayonets oaptured at Balipara and two rifles taken at Tonga river were given up. Our casualties were 4 men killed and seven wounded ; the Akas suffered no casualties. The foroe did not remain in the hills long enough to

impress the people but retired almost immediately with- out imposing any fine, or burning any village. A half-hearted blookade of the Frontier was kept up till 1888 when the Akas came in and on professing submis- sion were pardoned. Since 1888 the Akas have been well behaved. In 1918-14 their oountiy was visited by the Political Offioer, Western Seotion, North-East Frontier, the most peaceful relations were established there and tire sur- rounding countries were mapped and explored. The Akas are divided into the following, clans : — 1. Kutson. 2. Kovatsun. 8. Karam. 4. Golu. 5. Nyobin. 11. Miri Aka. 6. Tepun. 7. Pushing. 8. Khosakhyon. 9. Gujeria 10. Dujia. The Akas are the upper class and have wider them a class known as Khoas. The Ehoas are a distinct community speaking a language of their own r they do most of the manual work of the country, and are paid for their work in kind ; they are not m any sense slaves. The Eutson and Eovatsun are the two most important of the olans. The headquarter village of the former is Jamiri and the latter Gonaintan. The clans live in distinct groups of villages called by the clan name. The villages are almost invariably built on the healthy sites offered by high flat topped spurs. They are usually small consisting of from 8 to 10 houses. The Eutson and Eovatsun clans dominate the rest, and in external affairs the heads of these two olans aot as Chiefs for the whole counter ; in dealing with , internal affairs they aot as presidents of the oouncils and have no more influence than their personality allows. Village questions are settled in open council, but those which affect tho whole clan or group of clans are settled by a council of village representatives meeting either at Jamiri or at Gohaintan. Every free man has the right of speech, but the method of debate often oonsists in shouting down dissentients. In oases of

doubt lots are cast. Women have considerable influ* ence, but it is exercised behind the scenes [as they are not allowed to speak at the village councils.* There is no slavery in the oountry. The Aka language is classified by Grierson as Language, belonging to Tibeto-Burman group but is very difficult to see any resemblance between it and Other dialeot of the same group. The Ehoa language is entirely distinct from that spoken by the Akas. 8 Apjmran e e ftud dress. The Akas arc a woll made strongly built race, yellowish brown and of a very Mongolian appearance. They are a platyoprosopic or a flat faced race, their hair is straight and black, the average height of the men is 6' 4", of the women under 5'. A man’s dross consists of a short coarse cotton cloth which is wound round the body and pinned over the shoulder by small bamboo pins, the garment is bound round, the waist by a kummerbund below which it forms a short skirt reaching to a little below the knees. A jacket is worn which Ireaohos to the hips, sometimes this jacket has sleeves, sometimes it is sleeveless ; often it is merely a cloth wound round the shoulders. The hair is twisted into a knot at the top of the head. The head dross is a curious pill box like hat made of split bamboo ubout four inches deep; in front is worn a bunch of feathers or dried bamboo leaves. The lobes of oars arc pierced, in them tho rich wear cylindrical pear shaped silvor earrings but the majority wear bamboo tubes. In his belt the Alca wears a dao, he also carries a bow and arrows slung across his hack. An Aka woman’s dross oonsists of a cloth wound round her waist similar to that worn by the man but reaching almost to the ankles. She wears a long jacket usually of Assamese silk. Her hair is done up in a knot at the back of her head and round the upper part of her forehead the well-to-do woman wears a very striking fillet of silver ohain work ; in her ears she wears earrings similar to those worn by the men, and round her neck innumerable neoklaees of coloured heads on which arc hung silver Tibetan ornaments. Both men and women wear cotton cloth gaiters to

proteot them from tho bites of Dam Dim (Simuleum Ittdicum), fastoned just below the knee with a string of blue beads, 0 Their houses are woll built wooden struotures of dressed timber raised off tho ground on piles and* roofed with thatch or palm leaves. The beams and joists arc carefully squared with an adze and are often roughly curved. Each house iB about 60 yds. long and 8 yds. wide. The houses are divided internally into 4 or 5 rooms with a wide verandah at each end. The front room is the guest room and in it are usually hung the heads of Mithan and wild animals to show the ^consequence of the host and his prowess in the chase. Theso people occupy the upper valley of the Bichom. Tho Mijis. 'I heir valley is rich and fertile and could easily support a muoh greater population than it does. The Mijis are closely akin to the Akas both in appearance and customs the two people constantly inler-marry. The Mijis have no chiefs but each rillago has its headman who possesses considerable authority within his village. Their language is different to that of the Aka. . The Miji trades freely with the Tibetans travelling vid. the Mago pass. The Miri Akas are a fairly largo tribe living on the Tho Mirl left bank of the Bichom river and also in the Kovu Akas. and Pachuk valleys. They are very closely related to the Aka, but they are a good deal less civilized, and are much dirtier. They act as a buffer between the Akas and the Dallas living to the north. They are friendly with both tribes. The Dallas inhabit the portion of the Himalaya The Data* from the Bhoreli river eastward to the Khru river, a tributary of the Subansiri river. They are a very large tribe, tney may roughly be divided into two mam divisions the YANO (or Yan) and the TAGEN . The meaning of the word Daffa is obscure, it is a name given to these people by the Assamese, it is not used amongst them, they refer to themselves in general terms as Bengni (men), but villages are usually called by the Nebu (khel) name. ' 10 Afpeuance, The Yano or Western Daflas inhabit the Hills from the Tibet border north of the Akas as far as the

Boroi river. East of the Boroi river and as far as the Ehru Biver live the Tagen. Daflas. The two peoples are very muoh alike in dress and appearance, but speak different dialects. The people are well made, plucky and very truculent. They have very independent manners which might often be taken for rudenoss by a stranger. They would be very formidable if there was any com- bination between them. There is however practically none though in the face of a great common danger it is possible that they might make common oause. Every village is a separate community living usually in a state of feud with its neighbours. The size of the village is regulated by the nature of the country ; if the cultivable area be large the village may be very largo also but as a rule 12 houses is the usual size. The houses are well built wooden structures built on changs, and roofed with thatch or palm leaves » they are very long — sometimes as much as 250 feet — and about 6 yards broad. Each house would oontain about 50 souls. The Daflas are divided into a great number of exogamous Nebus or kbels such as Bod, Nabbum, Nitung, Tabba, Taohing, Bao, Tao, Tagen and many others. The Daflas are short well formed men of consider- able muscular development, with large broad flat faoes, high cheek bones, and large mouth. They have no hair on cheeks or chins. Many of the Tagen Daflas tattoo their faoes, the western very rarely tattoo. On the head a cane work helmet with a plume of ions bill feathers is worn. A cloth is worn on the body and tied crossways in front over the arms. The hair is done up in a knot on the forehead, through this knot isthrast a brass pin about nine inches long. The sword is slung round the neck by a belt often deoorated with oowrie shells. 11 A long straight dao in a bamboo scabbard, a bow, Arm*, a quiver full of arrows, many of them iron tipped and oovered with ooncoction of aconite and pigs fat, which forms a very deadly poison. When travelling or raiding they oarry a long spear. Their method of cultivation is by j 'hunting or Cultivation, felling and burning the forest, it is then picked over and cleaned and the earth stirred with a sharp bamboo. The staple crops are hill rice, maize, millet, jobs tears, tobacco and chillies.

The Dafla hills, taken generally, are a very broken The oountry mass of mountains, rugged and difficult ; the valleys become larger and the slope easier as the snowy range is approached. There are however some very fertile tracts and here the villages are large and close together. Such are the Ehru river, Miri pathar, the Popum river, the Dikrang river and the Banganadi. This latter river is oapable of supporting a very large popu- lation as it is open oountry with large undulating grassy valleys. The Banganadi is the only known portion of the Dafla hills where terraced rice cultivation exists. The Dafla is by religion an animist. He believes Betigiou . in the good and evil spirits of nature, and is constantly employed in trying to placate the Evil Spirits of the winds, the forest, the mountains, etc. The benign spirits do not trouble him as they, are well disposed ana need no humouring. In every village there is more than one Nvobn or Deodbai who is constantly consulting omens and sacrificing to appease offended spirits. Omens are taken on all occasions, suoh as before making a raid, a journey, contracting a marriage, at a birth and a death. The Dallas have from the first mention we have History, of them been known as a clamorous and turbulent people. Of them wrote Mahomed Zazim in the day of Aurungseb, “ The Dallas are entirely independent of the Assam Baja, and whenever they find an omnor- tunity plunder the country contiguous to tneir mountains.** 12 From the beginning of our occupation of Assam the Daflas gave much trouble to our local offioers, as in tho days of the Assam llajahs the Daflas were given the right to collect from every ten houses one double cloth, one single cloth, one handkerchief, one dao, ten head of horned cattle, and four seers of salt. Tho Assamese living along the Frontier who were thus taxed paid only Us. 3 instead of Its. 9 from each got to the Gov- ernment. Tho Daflas collected these duos in full and were guilty of many acts of oppression in doing so. These raids caused so much irritation that in 1873 a military force attempted to blockade the Hills in order to prevent any Daflas coming to the Fl&ins. The blockade proving inefficient a military force was sent into the Bills on a punitive expedition. This had the effect of causing the Daflas to keep quiet for a few years. Since then the Daflas have constantly broken the peace ; details will be found in Mackenzie's North-East Frontier and Oaptain St. John MiohelTs reports. Several expeditions have visited the Hills and the hillmen have now learned that their Hills are not utterly inaooessible to our sepoys as they once believed. 13 Praotically all raids bare been against Dallas settled in the plains to avenge, what the hillmen believed to be, very just grievances and with no idea that they were disturbing the peace of the British Raj. These people inhabit a magnificent plateau some The Apa ten miles long and six mile* broad laid out in highly Tanan s 8 - cultivate 1 and artificially irrigated terraoes well watered by the Kali river, a sluggish stream some 45 to 60 feet in breadth with low alluvial banks. Tho hills surrounding tho valley rise to some 1,500 to 2,000 feot above the level of the Kali river the slopes are covered with fine pine forests. The people live in large villages — they may almost be called towns — a* Hong, the largest village, contains 2,000 houses. The men are well made averaging about 6' 6". They wear their hair like Dafias dono up in front in a knot about tho forehead, through this knot is< passed a brass pin about T' long. The clothing consists of a cloth worn round the waist and brought up and secured ovor the shoulders whilst over this is worn a square blanket of blue and red striped cloth fastonod by with a loop and buttoned round the neck. Round the waist is worn a curious contrivanoe made of thin strips of oane dyed a bright scarlet, the cane is formed into a tail bohind about 18" long. The women wear a abort skirt of coloured oottou and a zouave jacket of like material. Their hair is done up in a knot on the top of thoir heads. In each

nostril they wear a round eylinder of wood about an inoh in diameter, which horribly disfigures features that would otherwise be pleasant or even comely. The Apa lanang or Ankas (tail), as they are locally oalled, are peaoeful agriculturists ; they live at peace with their neighbours and the size of their villages protects them from outside raids. They have a strong tribal feeling and if attaoked they would quiokly concentrate in order to avenge themselves. 14 The Hill Miris. Their system of irrigation is excellent, the whole yalley is under cultivation, the distribution of water is very oleverly managed and shows a high degree of organization. On the surrounding hills excellent crops of maize, millet, jobs tears, etc., are grown. Bamboos are cultivated for building purposes and the felling of timber both for building and firewood is carefully regulated. When a block of timber is out for firewood, tho wood is stacked and then issued, as the forests are cut blocks of equal size are aforested. Their plantations being carefully tended and fenoed round as a guard against cattlo. The valley is governed by a council of elders who wield considerable authority. The population is probably about 20,000. They are very well off as they sell their superfluous crops to their surrounding neighbours. Their language differs very considerably from Dafla or Miri. They are a peaceful people and have only once, in 1896 given trouble, on this occasion they raided and murdered some Hill Miris settled in the plains who they alleged cheated them. A Military Expedition visited their valley shortly after, since then they have been very peaceful. The Hill Miris inhabit the Subansiri valley as far as the plains. They must in no way be confounded with the Miris living in the plains of Assam, the latter are descended from men of the Dafla, Hill Miri and Abor tribes who have in times past left the hills and settled in the plains, and have now become a distinct community. They are divided into several dans, Baraks, Pani* botia, Tarbotia and Ghasis. 15

Tlie Panibotia, Tabotia and Sarahs are fine tall men of great mosoular strength, they are better looking and slightly more civilized than their Dafla neighbours. The Ghasi are a small people and not so civilized as the other Miris. The Miri villages average about 20 houses, their houses are built on ohanga anl closely resemble those built by the Dallas. These people are capable of concentration against a common foe and for that reason they are not raided by their neighbours, and lead a peaceful existence. They are well behaved and have never given us any trouble. We have always been on most friendly terms with them. The Poaa of Rs. 2,241-12-8 which we pay them is more perhaps of a charity than any wo pay on the North-East Erontier. Their country was visited in 1911-12 by the Miri Mission. This distriot consists of terai and hill tracts, both sparsely populated. The terai is unhealthy like all other tracts lying under the hills in Assam. Fever is prevalent and kala agar has appeared. The hill tracts are free from fever, although many cases oocur of fever contracted in the plains. From time to time there are outbreaks of small-pox. Cholera is very rare. In- fluenza has remained in the hills since the outbreak of 1919, though it has assumed a milder form. On the whole, compared with other parts of Assam, the district is healthy, as is shewn by the 6th Assam Rifles being the healthiest of the^B Battalions stationed in the different hill districts of Assam. In the hills infant mortality aooounts for the greater number of deaths. Amongst the Akas consumption oaused chiefly by the insufficient ventilation of their houses is distressingly common. Vital statu- Vital statistics are not reported. The birth-rate except m ' amongst the Akas and plains Daflas is higher than the death-rate and tbe population is on the increase ; the inorease would be very large but for the heavy infant mortality. The general health of the plains people is. goods exoept amongst tbe Daflas. These are all men who have left the hardships and hazards of the hills and settled in the plains where they lead a peaceful and more luxurious life. They are not used to tbe olimate and malaria makes great ravages amongst them. HpidamioR Small-pox is not endemic in ths hills hut outbreaks oocur from time to time oaused by infection from the g mm. p] a j Q8i these outbreaks, 'apart from the deaths due to them, cause much trouble, for whenever a bill village contracts the disease it invariably accuses another village nearer to the plains, of bringing in the disease and, that village is promptly raided. This leads to retaliation, and often the casualties arising from these raids are- more numerous than the deaths oaused bjr the small-pox. 21 Malaria is naturally very prevalent in all the plains villages, as they are all situated in the unhealthy low- lying terai. In the hills malaria is not common, snoh oases as ooour being oontracted by persons who have been visiting or working in the plains. The hill Dafla Is much more proof against malaria than the Tibetan, Bhutanese or Momba. Goitre is very oommon in the hills, more especially in villages where the water-supply runs through cultivation. In villages where the water comes from a rocky spring, a oommon source in the

Aka country, no goitre will be found. Pneumonia is very oommon and is probably oaused by the smoke and bad ventilation of the houses. Diarrhoea is fairly oommon. Cholera outbreaks are very rare. ^Venereal diseases are unknown at present amongst the hill Akas and Daflas, but a few cases have ooourred, amongst the plains Daflas. With the Tibetans and Mombas, who are next-door neighbours, venereal disease of all descriptions is very common. Kala aear is reported to be on the increase amongst the plains population. So far it is almost entirely con- fined to the Assamese and Kacharis. Oases are being sought out and treated and all head men have strict orders to report cases.
